#79676. Latest Update: Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (595 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22.
  • Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
  • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My blueprint is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he remarked.

Sources indicate that lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

In a recent development, neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

The Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch intends to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line right now being attempted by a Russian team.

This is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

According to recent reports, simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his aims while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

#79674. Deer Hunting Has Never Been Easier Than Right Now

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1091 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Deer Hunting Has Never Been Easier Than Right Now

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1091 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been hunting whitetail deer for about 20 years now, and I can still remember what hunting a low deer density, heavy hunting pressure area was like.
  • It wasn’t until about 10 years ago that I started noticing a change.
  • According to recent reports, but it’s not just in my area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been hunting whitetail deer for about 20 years now, and I can still remember what hunting a low deer density, heavy hunting pressure area was like. When I was a kid, more than 1 million hunters would enter the woods and hunt Pennsylvania’s opening day of rifle season. In my heavily populated area, I always saw a lot more hunters than I did deer.

It wasn’t until about 10 years ago that I started noticing a change. The deer population was skyrocketing and it hasn’t slowed down. Paired with a decline in the hunting population, I’ve experienced the highest deer numbers of my life recently.

According to recent reports, but it’s not just in my area. The population has soared across the vast majority of the whitetail’s range, making it easier and easier for us remaining hunters to fill our tags. Tack on the crazy advancements in technology like cellular trail cameras, the latest crossbows, and even technologically-advanced compound bows, and I truly believe deer hunting has never been easier than right now. Here’s why that’s a good thing — sort of.

According to recent reports, across the whitetail’s range, populations are at an all time high. That’s not just my opinion — it’s fact.

“There are between 30 to 35 million whitetails in the U.S. right now,” notes Kip Adams, chief conservation officer for the National Deer Association. “That’s a crazy number of deer on the landscape. And, the harvest data is backing that up. Nationally, we’ve only surpassed three million bucks harvested annually four times in the last century, all of which occurred within the last five years. We also have the best age structure in the last 100 years. So we’re killing more bucks, and older bucks than ever before.”.

The good news here is that the increasing population has been met with increases in opportunity from the tag allocation side, and the harvest data proves those opportunities are working.

“We have expanded seasons across the board, higher bag limits than any point in the last century, and more advanced weapons to fill those tags,” indicates Adams. “If you can’t shoot a deer today, you just really aren’t trying very hard.”.

Now, before you go grabbing your pitchforks because you’re still sitting on a pile of tags this season, it’s worth mentioning that Adams and I both agreed that it’s never been easier to kill any deer, but we’re certainly not implying it’s easy to kill a specific deer.

In a recent development, it’s also worth noting that certain areas across the whitetail’s range have seen a decrease in opportunities as diseases like CWD and EHD have impacted herd numbers, and habitat loss continues with urban expansion. But, for most of the whitetail’s range, opportunities abound.

It has been revealed that I’ll be the first to admit I love my cell cameras. I check them almost too often this time of year, but that immediate satisfaction and data grab is addicting. And, that data has helped me dial in the movement patterns of the deer herd in my area based on weather conditions in ways that standard SD card cameras couldn’t. That information, when applied correctly, makes filling a tag substantially easier than just guessing and trying to get lucky.

Industry observers note that take the buck my father tagged last year for example. We had gotten a few photos of him in velvet, keying us in on the area he was using. After planning to stay out of the area and wait for mid to late October when the buck started hitting scrapes, we sat back and waited. Around Oct. 21, we got our first photo of him in the area. And he stayed consistent for three days, hitting the scrape every evening in daylight. On the fourth night, we went in, set up, and a shot opportunity presented itself.

Sure, the stars had to align and the conditions had to be just right for that pattern to exist, but without the technological advancements to trail cameras, I don’t know if we would have gotten a chance at that buck.

Tack on the advancements in our gear. From compounds to crossbows, inlines to straight-walls, and even modern cartridge design, we’ve never been better equipped to shoot deer with more accuracy and efficacy.

“Almost all states in the whitetail’s range allow crossbows for everyone now,” Adams says. “Plus, more and more states that used to be shotgun only are now allowing straight-wall cartridges or inline muzzleloaders. All of those additions make it easier for hunters to fill their tags.”.

Industry observers note that while the pros speak for themselves, the cons come down to more of an opinion than anything rooted in fact. I have to wonder what all this ease is doing to the heritage of hunting. Hunting was never about being easy, in fact, I’d argue the opposite. It was about the thrill of the chase, the reward of filling your tag after a long season, putting your woodsmanship to the test and coming out on top, and the conservation of one of America’s most valuable resources.

I grew to love hunting because it was challenging. I was unsuccessful a lot, which put a fire in my belly to learn more, hunt harder, and find a way to be successful through the lessons I learned along the way. I wonder if kids like me are getting the same experience, and what the hook for them might be if not.

There’s also the ethical dilemma that an easier hunting experience brings. From the ethics and fair-chase argument relating to cellular trail cameras, to the liberal weapon usage and even baiting tactics in certain states, I fear we’re very close to crossing the line into an unfair advantage over our quarry, if we haven’t gotten there already.

Read Next: Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back.

It’s up to us as the hunters, and up to the states to decide how much is too much of a good thing. And as the deer populations continue to expand, I personally don’t see a world where the states are the ones that are going to draw the line. So, this season, as you continue to chase that major buck or a nice doe for the freezer, ask yourself where you plan to draw the line. And, feel free to join me in wondering how it’s still possible to struggle to fill a tag from time to time.

#79670. Breaking: The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1234 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1234 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one.
  • What I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first.
  • Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It demonstrated again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

What I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

In a recent development, after 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang said: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:.

Recent findings suggest that several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

In a recent development, strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

“Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

“Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”.

It has been revealed that when they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

Sources indicate that during their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s proposal to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:.

Sources indicate that on October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

Industry observers note that “From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”.

In the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

“Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”.

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

According to recent reports, “Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”.

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

“We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang remarked. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

Recent findings suggest that strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”.

The climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai.

It has been revealed that the problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

The climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

Climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

According to recent reports, rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”.

Strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

On many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he says:.

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

In a recent development, the climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After my very dark dome day, I went to bed feeling proud of myself but worried that I’d wake up feeling equally tired.
  • Notes from the trail log at the dome cafe (no longer actually a cafe).
  • According to recent reports, we had been discussing “trail legs” for a couple of days now, wondering if maybe we were finally getting them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After my very dark dome day, I went to bed feeling proud of myself but worried that I’d wake up feeling equally tired. Much to my delight, however, I slept well and woke up feeling pretty restored. It’s amazing what a shower, some food, and a sleep will do for your body.

Notes from the trail log at the dome cafe (no longer actually a cafe).

According to recent reports, we had been discussing “trail legs” for a couple of days now, wondering if maybe we were finally getting them. I think on this day I got my first inkling of them, we walked as a group this morning (except Charlie who we knew would catch up as she’s the fastest out of all of us) and zoomed through the first ten kilometres. It was easy gravel road and the clouds hadn’t burned off yet. I felt good despite how hard I’d found the day before.

Sinèad, Annabel and I stopped for a snack break before the final hill portion of the day. The sun had started to burn off the clouds at this point, and it was starting to get hot. But we knew we only had about 15km into Puhoi (where we’d find food and maybe even a beer), and a campsite in 10km where we could replenish our water. So we pushed on.

Industry observers note that this section of the day was a slog, not because the terrain was hard (it was just a gravel road) but because the sun was so hot. Saying we were sweaty would be an understatement, but there was nowhere to stop to cool off because the whole track was exposed. So we pushed on.

At some point Charlie did catch us and we all continued our climb up the gravel hill. This was the moment that I really decided that my merino hoodie was going to have to go. Luckily I have Fraser at home with access to my lighter-weight synthetic sun hoodies so I got him to send one to my friend in Auckland. Feels nice to not have to spend money unnecessarily.

Eventually, like finding an oasis in a desert, we spotted a little side track that led to a grassy, shaded area. I made a beeline for it and dropped all my stuff. It was approaching noon and I decided it was lunch time so took off my sun hoodie and pulled out my remaining trail pizza ingredients. This break was such a relief!

After drinking about half a litre of water and eating my two wraps (this time with added chilli flavoured corn nuts for crunch), I felt fortified enough to keep walking in the sun.

The rest of the afternoon passed in a sweaty blur and soon we found ourselves descending a strange path between two paddocks toward the Remiger road campsite at km 533. At this point I had pretty much run out of water so I powered ahead, focused on the water tank I knew was at the camp. It was a beautiful camp with a nice shelter, and after our 20 very hot kilometres it was a really great place for a break.

Sources indicate that we had decided the night before that we’d try to make it into Puhoi and the call of the pub was strong enough to keep us from pitching tents at Remiger road. After a decent, shoe off, stretch out kind of break we were ready to conquer the final 4.5km of road walking.

It has been revealed that with eternal hope in our hearts, we gave hitching a go, but people only sped up when they saw us. Thanks, Auckland.

Industry observers note that once we realized that hitching wasn’t going to happen, we began our road walk to Puhoi. It went surprisingly quickly and soon Charlie was dancing and waving her poles out front of the Puhoi tea rooms.

According to recent reports, annabel, Charlie, me and Sinèad at the tea rooms after checking in. Photo courtesy of Sinèad.

The tea rooms were our home for the night, for $10 you get a very non-private shower (but there’s hot water so I’m not complaining), wifi, charging, and a tent site. The owner also does a special offer for TA hikers where he re-opens the cafe just for us and will make you anything off the menu or a burger. This seemed much nicer than walking a further 500m to the pub and was probably also cheaper, so we all agreed to stay in for the night.

We also met up with Moritz who had taken a zero at the tea rooms. He was full of energy and went to the shop to buy us snacks and used his flip fuel to top up our gas canisters. Before I left for Te Araroa I told Fraser I was sure I’d meet someone who would be able to do that, and once again: the trail provides.

I went to bed full and happy, and with the knowledge that because of tides, we’d have a very slow morning and then a chill 8km kayak down the Puhoi river the next day.

Recent findings suggest that with our kayaks booked at 1pm, we had a slow morning. I had time to blog, charge all my electronics, dry my tent and order my blasphemous breakfast (see blog post about food for more). It was a luxurious morning and included coffee!!

At about 11:30am we headed toward the pub and general store where I did a small resupply and got some lunch and another coffee. I was not messing around with coffee anymore, not after how I felt on the dome day.

In a recent development, at 1pm, we made our way to the kayak place, got our briefing, and dropped off our packs. The awa (river) is the official TA trail, which is pretty cool! It requires an outgoing tide, so the moon and ocean and river decide what time your day starts. It felt sort of lovely to know that we didn’t have a choice of when we started. The awa has long served as a highway for waka (boats) and its name translates to “slow water”.

The awa is aptly named, and the kayak down it was so peaceful. I spent a lot of time just being carried by the current and paddling intermittently only to steer. Though the highway now runs over and beside the awa, it’s still a lovely space. As I paddled down, I watched the water turn from a murky brown river to clear, salinated ocean water.

Industry observers note that A penguin floated past and I desperately tried to point it out for the people behind me. As I approached the end of the river, I spotted rays. It was magical.

Sources indicate that once off the kayaks, everyone agreed that it would be rude not to swim. So we got in the now ocean water. It was refreshing, and so warm compared to the water I’m used to swimming in in Wellington. The ground, however, was a whole strange experience. I spent most of the swim trying to keep my feet from touching the gooey mud on the bottom and Annabel and I screamed as our feet sank in.

It was a nice, silly afternoon.

Soon we were all back in our dry clothes, socks and dry-ish shoes. We stated bye to Anica who was nursing an Achilles injury, which was sad.

Recent findings suggest that there wasn’t much left in the day and we’d have to wait for a tidal section on the other side of a small hill. We set off anyway, and got our legs back into the habit of walking after our lazy morning and kayak.

On top of the hill between the end of the Puhoi and Waiwera.

By the time we reached Waiwera (which translates to hot water because of the hot springs in the area) Charlie and I were not feeling keen to wait for the tides. My beach-blisters were hurting and making me feel like I was limping, and Charlie was just generally not feeling well. We decided to split up, and she and I took a bus into Ōrewa to check us all into the campground while the other two waited for the tides.

Charlie on the bus – she has a very similar shot of me.

It has been revealed that the Ōrewa holiday park was by far the worst place we’ve stayed. The “tent sites” were actually just hard-packed ground with a ton of tree roots. But the staff were really nice and I decided I’d ask at the office how much it would cost to upgrade to a cabin (it ended up being $1.25 extra each). I’m so glad I did!! There were some strange characters at the park and one guy told us that his laundry had been stolen the night before, so it felt nice to have a lock on the door.

Our little cabin was soon full of tents drying out, and dry bags jammed into every corner. We pondered whether we could fit Moritz in on the floor but luckily another hiker, Tim, had booked the cabin beside ours so he got a real bed.

What else would thru-hikers do at night.

I was happy to leave Ōrewa, and knew we were heading for a big supermarket and shopping mall. The walk this morning was easy and quick into Silverdale, where we all split up to run our respective errands. I spent way too much money buying blister plasters and restocking my supplements at chemist warehouse, but offset that by NOT buying a pastry at the coffee shop.

Caffeinated and ready to go, we packed up our latest things and started the walk to Stillwater. This was all road and started relatively pleasantly with wide sidewalks and grassy shoulders. But eventually we got on the final stretch of road to Stillwater and it became the worst road we had encountered on the whole trail so far. Big trucks blasted past us and we scrambled to not fall into the steep ditches. When we finally came to a spot where someone could pick us up, Annabel, Sinèad and I decide to try to hitch.

Charlie, being ever the bravest of us, continued along the road and remarked the road did eventually get better.

A lovely couple picked us up and started telling us about a cabin we could stay in along the Ōkura walkway. This led to them calling their daughter who noted that the cabin was SO FAR into the walk, like thirty minutes. We all laughed out loud at that and then she asked her mum to send her $32. Walking the bulk of that scary road was made worth it by that one phone call.

The couple dropped us off at the end of the road, and we ate our lunch at a little park before joining the Ōkura walkway. We got lucky with tides and were able to skirt the edges of the coast for this walk and very quickly found ourselves at Dacre Cottage. This was a gorgeous campsite with a shelter, toilets, water and some pretty nice, flat spaces to pitch tents. We were there early but the next kilometre or so involved a tidal crossing and it wasn’t low tide until 8pm. We would have to wait until the morning and cross at low tide.

Sources indicate that once again the TA fearmongering began. We had received videos from Sven who crossed a day or two before us showing everyone in their undies with the water up to their chests. I decided it would be fun even if it was meant to rain tomorrow. And besides, we all had indoor beds booked tomorrow night so it didn’t matter if all our stuff got soaked, right?

A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains.
  • In a recent development, the two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition.
  • Though suffering from stomach problems for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a upcoming route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains. Reaching up to 5,509m, the once-unknown granite cliffs now draw dozens of international climbers each summer. The two core valleys, Ak-Su and Kara-Su, have become known as Central Asia’s Patagonia.

In a recent development, the two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition. First, a summary of their four weeks.

Though suffering from stomach problems for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a upcoming route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.

Three climbers — Bruno Crljenic, Eva Pejic, and Lackovic — identified a potential upcoming line below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They knew of only one previous route on the mountain, done by Russians Marina Popova and Denis Prokofiev.

Crossing a scree slope on Pik Breeze.

Recent findings suggest that beginning at 5am, the three crossed a broad scree slope, then began climbing a couloir below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They negotiated loose rock, briefly followed an existing line, then moved left into crack systems.

Canned Horse, 6c A0, top. Below, previous attempts and possible other lines on the face.

They climbed until 9pm, when they bivouacked on a tiny ledge with space for only two people sitting and one lying down. Resuming at 8:30am, they reached a col after three pitches and continued directly up slabs and cracks. They finished on easier IV/V terrain and followed a 200m ridge to the summit.

Recent findings suggest that they called their new line Canned Horse, 930m, 23 pitches, 6c A0. It took them a further eight hours to get back to base camp. During the climb, they found pitons on two pitches. They believe these belonged to another route on the west ridge, but the history of that line, and whether it was finished, is uncertain.

Pejic, Grbac Lackovic, and Crljenic on top of Pik Breeze.

It has been revealed that later in the month, one of those climbers, Eva Pejic, became quite ill and couldn’t leave base camp on her own. Five teammates helped evacuate her, carrying her for 11km, with assistance from other climbers in the area. She later recuperated in the Kyrgyz city of Osh.

On the first crux of ‘Perestroika Crack.’.

Three small teams of Croatian climbers also repeated Perestroika Crack, one of the best-known long granite routes in Central Asia. It rises about 900m up the north face of 4,240m Pik Slesova and is graded 7a. Three members reportedly free-climbed the route. One pair, Sinisa Skalec and Ivan Vitez, completed the line in a single marathon day, beginning at 5:45am, summiting at 5:40pm, and returning to base camp at 11pm.

It has been revealed that skalec and Vitez also repeated the French Ridge of 4,510m Kyrkchilta, 2,000m, 6b to 6b+. They needed one bivouac. Toward the end of August, this same pair attempted a first ascent on the Central Pyramid of Ortotyubek, overlooking base camp. Their attempted route mounted slabs and cracks to the left of the established Take It Easy line, which other Croatians had repeated during that month. The pair gave up their attempt on August 26 because of illness.

Base camp with Ortotyubek and Slesova in the background.

Here is our interview with Lukas Grbac Lackovic and Sinisa Skalec about Kyrgyzstan and the Ak-Su Valley.

Lukas Grbac Lackovic repeats the Central Route on a peak called Small Russian Tower.

Was Eva Pejic’s health problem related to altitude or something else? What was the illness you experienced on Ortotyubek?

According to recent reports, eva’s health problem was unrelated to altitude exposure or the expedition environment. However, most of us experienced gastrointestinal infections, with symptoms including diarrhea, bloating, fever, and general malaise.

According to recent reports, this significantly hindered our climbing, as everyone in the team got sick at least once, and some even twice. Recovery was slow and never quite complete –- we felt weak for most of the trip.

One thing that helped us recover was having plain rice with some of our meals, which we could get from the cook if we asked nicely. If we were to go again, we would definitely bring our own food and cooking equipment. This can be inconvenient, but it could potentially save you at least a week of being sick and unable to climb.

Another view of base camp and peaks Ortotyubek and Slesova.

Can you describe the Karavshin Valley? How large is it? Are there many side valleys?

Industry observers note that the two main valleys are Ak-Su and Kara-Su. Adjacent to them is the Jaupaya Valley, which provides a descent route from Pik Breeze and is home to several peaks around 5,000m high. The rock quality there appears poor, and we are not aware of any established rock routes in the valley.

In a recent development, another interesting area, west of Kara Su, is the Orto-Chashma Gorge. An Italian team made a first ascent there during our visit.

Here in the West, we first heard about the area following the kidnapping of four American climbers in Kara-Su in 2000. Since then, it seems to have calmed down and become a popular climbing destination. Is the area considered safe nowadays, or are there still things climbers should be aware of?

Recent findings suggest that currently, the security situation in the valley is good. There is always the possibility of tensions, of course, as the valleys lie close to the border with Tajikistan. However, in recent years, the number of climbers visiting the area has increased exponentially, reaching around 100 climbers this year.

It has been revealed that how many other climbing teams were in Ak-Su and neighboring Kara-Su while you were there? Where were they generally from?

Sources indicate that during the three weeks we spent in the valley, up to 50 climbers were in BC at the same time. Climbers came from all over the world — Chile, U.S., Spain, Slovakia, Poland, Belgium, Slovenia, France, Italy, Germany, Japan, Russia….

Why did your group decide to go there?

It has been revealed that we had originally planned a different expedition, but had to change our destination just a few months before departure. Some friends from Croatia and Slovenia recommended the area because of its straightforward logistics and relatively good security, while still offering impressive big walls and proper crack climbing. It didn’t take much to convince us!

Are there any military checkpoints? Do you need special permission to enter the valleys?

Sources indicate that yes, you have to pass through a military checkpoint when entering the area. However, the outfitter handles the application for the necessary permits and ensures everything goes smoothly.

Some call the Karavshin Valley the Patagonia of Central Asia because of its aesthetic granite walls. Do you think that’s a fair description?

Patagonia is definitely more spectacular, but you pay the price with poor weather. If your goal is to climb almost every day, then the Karavshin Valley is a better choice.

Sources indicate that climbing in Patagonia requires much more logistical planning and preparation, and the approaches themselves are a whole different story. In the Karavshin Valley, on the other hand, there is no snow or ice during the season we visited (August), at least on the walls we climbed. Some of the walls are just a 15-minute walk from BC, and you can reach them all in approach shoes.

Perestroika Crack and some of the classic routes in the Karavshin region are arguably just as good as the best rock routes in Patagonia.

How does the granite compare to Yosemite and Patagonia?

It has been revealed that the granite is more similar in texture to that found in Patagonia; it is not as smooth as in Yosemite. The overall rock quality is generally good, although, as everywhere, some sections are of poorer quality. One downside of the mild climate in the Karavshin Valley is the dirt and grass that accumulate in the cracks, which can sometimes detract from the aesthetic appeal of the routes. The more popular and frequently climbed routes have already been cleaned and are pleasant to climb.

In a recent development, you climbed 4-1/2 pitches of the route on Ortotyubek. How much did you have left to complete it?

There were still two-and-a-half pitches left to complete the route up to the junction with Take It Easy. We envisioned the second half of the fifth pitch following the line up to a point just below the overhang that runs diagonally to the left.

According to recent reports, from there, the sixth pitch follows a thin crack, from which you need to traverse left and move into another system of thin cracks that runs across the roof and joins the Take It Easy belay (seventh pitch). The last pitch of Take It Easy offers a logical exit, and we don’t think there is any need to come up with an alternative.

In a recent development, at the point where we stopped (first half of the fifth pitch), we left two pitons that we used as a temporary rappel anchor. Repeating parties are welcome to remove them, as they were only left for temporary use. We think a few bolts may be needed in the second half of the fifth pitch, but that obviously depends on the abilities of those planning to complete the route.

Industry observers note that all belays are equipped (the first and fourth belays have two 8mm bolts each, while the second and third have two pitons each). In addition, we left two or three pitons in the first pitch and two in the second pitch.

As in the rest of the valley, some sections of the route are filled with dirt and grass. We made an effort to clean the cracks in the first four pitches, but there is still plenty of work to be done, especially on the sixth pitch, which we didn’t climb, where a thin crack is completely filled with dirt.

Industry observers note that how much unclimbed rock remains? Are the obvious lines already established, or are there still many promising routes?

In a recent development, the most obvious and accessible lines may have already been climbed, but there is still plenty of potential. Anyone willing to put in the effort can establish a new route. The area is vast, and there is still plenty of room for new routes.

Sources indicate that your website mentions that there are guidebooks to certain routes in that area. Where are these available?

Most of the guidebooks we used are available online. We received some Russian guidebooks from climbing friends, although we didn’t use them very much. We’re not sure how easily they can be found online. Climbers from all over the world bring various materials to the camp, so most route topos and information can be obtained there.

What was the most unexpected experience on your expedition — something that might surprise climbers familiar with other significant-wall areas?

We were pleasantly surprised by the kindness and honesty of the Kyrgyz people. When traveling to remote parts of the world, many of us tend to expect that someone will try to rip us off and that we will have to haggle over everything, but that was not the case here.

Although some things took longer than expected, everything we had agreed on in advance was respected, and all the logistics for transportation and accommodation worked very well.

As we mentioned earlier, our only complaint concerns the food and hygiene conditions at the camp, which were most likely responsible for the digestive problems experienced by virtually all the climbers staying there.

#79662. ‘Full Panic Mode.’ Bowhunter Tags the 205-Inch Louisiana Buck His Family Followed for 3 Seasons

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (600 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

‘Full Panic Mode.’ Bowhunter Tags the 205-Inch Louisiana Buck His Family Followed for 3 Seasons

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for three years brothers Zack and Daniel Halbert of Bossier Parish, Louisiana, watched a nontypical buck grow into an incredible 200-class deer.
  • According to recent reports, “We never got a chance to shoot him last year,” Zack tells Outdoor Life.
  • It was clear this was the season to try to kill him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for three years brothers Zack and Daniel Halbert of Bossier Parish, Louisiana, watched a nontypical buck grow into an incredible 200-class deer. They kept tabs on the buck with trail cameras and debated when it was time to shoot the high and wide whitetail.

According to recent reports, “We never got a chance to shoot him last year,” Zack tells Outdoor Life. “Over last summer when he was still in velvet we saw on cameras that his rack had completely blown up and got huge, with lots of palmation.”.

It was clear this was the season to try to kill him. The brothers hunted hard during a 23-day stint in October, with one of them in a stand every day.

Sources indicate that “I was just the lucky one sitting that day when the buck slipped up,” claims Zack, a business-studies student at Louisiana Tech University. “My brother, dad, and I put in a lot of work hunting that buck. I would not have taken this deer without their help.”.

The Halberts had multiple setups around their 80-acre hunting property. Zack took the buck from a ground blind on a 48-degree morning in late October.

“The blind faced the woods, and I’m looking one way out a window, then leaned the other way, and there he was at 21 yards,” Zack claims. “It’s crazy how you can go from calm and in two seconds go into full panic mode.”.

Industry observers note that zack watched the buck for three long minutes as he waited for a broadside shot. When the buck finally turned, he drew and held at full draw for about 15 seconds. Then he let fly.

The buck took off, and Zack watched where it disappeared into the woods. Then he called his brother, dad, and girlfriend with the news.

Sources indicate that “When I shot I was so pumped I almost shook the ground blind over. Before I got out of the blind I was trying to stop shaking enough to finish my prayer for what a blessing it was.”.

Zack began trailing the deer into timber, but the blood became faint and he decided it would be best to call in a tracking dog.

“I didn’t want to mess up on this deer,” he says.

Tracker Eric Perry and his dog, Blue, arrived that evening.

According to recent reports, “It was getting toward dusk when the dog got there and was put on the buck’s trail,” Zack states. “Blue found it in just 15 minutes. The arrow was a good hit, but there was no exit hole and so not a good blood trail.”.

The deer had died in a creek, and Zack had to wade into the cold water to get his buck out. The crew dragged the deer out of the timber and loaded it into a truck and headed home. Zack estimates it was 5½ years old, and Buckmasters scorer Chris Bates measured Zack’s buck at 205 3/8 inches.

Although Buckmasters has a different scoring system than the one used by Boone and Crockett and Pope and Young Clubs (and therefore scores aren’t apples-to-apples), it’s worth noting that the largest nontypical killed with a bow in the state scored, according to P&Y records, 206 5/8 inches. That deer was taken in January 2012 by Alton McLead.

“I know my grandpa Dan, who isn’t with us anymore,” says Zack, “wouldn’t have believed his eyes if he got to see this deer.”.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (799 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions.
  • With the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season.
  • Industry observers note that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions. An American off-piste skier died in the Austrian Alps last weekend after he triggered a small slab avalanche. It was far too small to bury him, but it carried him into an open crevasse below.

With the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season. Last year, 151 people died in avalanches in Europe between October 2025 and June 2026, according to the European Avalanche Warning Service (EAWS), a shockingly high number.

Industry observers note that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland. It was the 13th most deadly year in the Alps since record-keeping began. It was also the highest tally ever since the “Winter of Terror” of 1951. Avalanche prevention standards have improved a lot since then, but the number of leisure skiers, climbers, and hikers in the mountains has multiplied as well. (Most of those 1951 victims lived in villages along avalanche paths.).

According to recent reports, last weekend’s accident took place at the Stubai Glacier ski resort. The glacier sections of the Alps typically open for skiing weeks earlier than other mountain resorts, thanks to their higher altitudes and glacial ice, which can provide good October skiing with just a thin layer of fresh snow on top. Stubai’s ski resort opened on October 9 this year.

In a recent development, A map of Stubai Glacier ski resort with the area where the accident happened circled in red. Photo: Stubaier Gletscher website.

According to recent reports, the skier was on his own, descending in an out-of-bounds area below East Daunkogel Peak at around 11:30am. His tracks on the snow show he eventually abandoned the snow-covered glacier and ventured onto a steeper, rocky area. At some point, he broke a small slab of crusty snow which dragged him some 50 meters into an open bergschrund, where he fatally fell 20 meters down, according to the Lawinen Report.

The accident site, with the skier’s tracks visible,  and the movement of the snow slab — 50m long and 25m wide — marked in pink. Photo: Lawinen Report.

It has been revealed that other skiers in the area saw the accident and raised the alarm, but the skier had died by the time they extracted him from the crevasse. The police said the slab was only 10cm to 30cm thick, and the slide was just 25 meters wide. The crevasse was 50 meters below the fracture point.

Avalanche risks are obvious on heavily loaded slopes, but the accident reveals that even a thin layer of unstable snow can cause a fatal fall. In this case, the snow had fallen recently on the verglass ice over glacier-polished smooth rocks, and had no time to settle. This is a typical early-season condition in mountain ranges around the world.

The accident occurred at nearly 3,000m of altitude on a shady northeast slope, where the snow hardly transforms and settles during the short days of late fall. To make things worse, the report notes that wind had picked up that morning, creating a weak crust on top of loose, cold, fresh snow, prone to breaking.

In a recent development, the avalanche site on the following day, with most of the terrain covered by freshly drifted snow. Photo: LWD Tirol.

The second factor was exposure: the skier might have easily survived the fall if the terrain had been a clean snow slope, but he was on rocky terrain, where a simple fall can result in serious injuries. Most of all, the crevasse below created what the report described as a “terrain trap.”.

Fans of backcountry and ski touring are eager to hit the slopes with the first snowflakes, and the scarcely covered terrain may provide a false sense of safety from avalanches. But objective dangers go beyond the significant powder avalanches and also include falls on icy slopes. In addition, the glaciers are dry after the summer, and the crevasses are wide open.

According to recent reports, after a mild fall, snow is falling heavily in the Alps this week, significantly improving conditions for the region’s ski resorts. Most of them blueprint to open this weekend. The snow will also offer backcountry opportunities, but conditions will remain highly unstable.

Snowfall up to two meters is expected today in the Alps. Graphic by meteoexploration.com.

The avalanche report today by the Tiroler Avalanche Service (LWD Tirol) reveals low risk in the Austrian mountains, a remarkable risk (3 out of 5) in the Swiss Alps, and moderate risk (2 out of 5) in France.

The avalanche forecast for today, November 19, in the Alps shows remarkable (level 3-orange) risk, especially in Switzerland. Graphic: LWD Tirol.

Alaska Considers ‘Unprecedented’ Closure of Public Land to Hunting, Trapping Along Controversial Ambler Road

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (586 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the state of Alaska may soon decide to close more than 400 square miles to hunting and trapping in anticipation of a controversial mining road.
  • While the Ambler Road itself has faced continuous opposition from hunting and conservation groups for its potential to fragment one of the largest remaining caribou herds, among other fish and habitat concerns, the recent development is creating even more consternation.
  • Recent findings suggest that “It’s unprecedented,” claims Mary Glaves, Alaska program manager for Backcountry Hunters and Anglers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the state of Alaska may soon decide to close more than 400 square miles to hunting and trapping in anticipation of a controversial mining road. The decision would be part of a push by the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority to build a road creating private access to a future mining district focused on copper and zinc deposits.

While the Ambler Road itself has faced continuous opposition from hunting and conservation groups for its potential to fragment one of the largest remaining caribou herds, among other fish and habitat concerns, the recent development is creating even more consternation.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s unprecedented,” claims Mary Glaves, Alaska program manager for Backcountry Hunters and Anglers. “We’re supposed to allow for balanced use of all of our resources. This would show preference to one resource over another.”.

Recent findings suggest that the proposal, which the Alaska Board of Game will consider during an online meeting Friday, would close 1 mile on either side of the 211-mile proposed road in northern Alaska to all hunting and trapping. It first became public in February and is part of a memorandum of understanding between several Alaskan native corporations and the state. The proposed closure is part of a “subsistence safeguard,” according to a story in the Alaska Beacon. Subsistence hunters could still cross through the road corridor to access other legal hunting grounds.

The hunting and trapping ban would begin July 1, 2029, and remain in place through at least Jan. 1, 2036, regardless of when or even if the road is built, Glaves says.

The Board of Game considered formalizing the MOU in a July meeting, and opposition was fierce, notes Glaves. Still, many Alaskan organizations could not prepare comment because the meeting was in the middle of fishing season. As a result, the board tabled the discussion until its formal meeting in January.

Recent findings suggest that A few months later, the Alaska Fish and Game commissioner announced another special meeting Nov. 20 to discuss the project, allowing only written public comment and no oral testimony.

“That isn’t illegal,” Glaves says, “but it’s not in the best interest of engaging the public.”.

Even more importantly, if the closure passes, it tells Alaskans that state public land can be shut down to access at the request of an anticipated industry and with no stated biological need.

In a recent development, the road has not been built, and there’s some question about whether or not Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the Democratic governor-elect, will support the project. He has not stated a position publicly but has said he will carefully evaluate money spent by the state. The Industrial Development and Export Authority, an economic development arm of the state, would be responsible for building the road. The Alaska Wilderness League, which opposes the project, estimates it could cost the state more than $2 billion including construction, maintenance, and financing.

The preemptive nature of the closure is particularly troubling to conservation groups.

Read Next: The Ambler Road Project Would Jeopardize One of the Last Great Wilderness Hunts in America.

“There is no compelling reason to establish these restrictions years before the project is constructed or in the absence of demonstrated need,” she wrote on Nov. 4. “Doing so would also set a troubling precedent of using the Board’s time and public resources to evaluate hypothetical impacts of projects that may never materialize, rather than addressing actual wildlife management and public access concerns as they arise.”.

  • His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police confirmed that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun. Chen disappeared November 8 on the main Yoshida Trail after continuing alone up 3,776m Mount Fuji during its closed season.

It has been revealed that his two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment. Chen continued on his own without crampons or sufficient cold-weather clothing. His last video was sent that morning between 2,300 and 2,700m.

His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Ironically, Chen belonged to China’s Blue Sky Rescue Team, a volunteer search-and-rescue organization. His mother told local media that he had participated in rescues in China and had some mountaineering experience, including trekking and climbing in Nepal and Indonesia.

#79654. Latest Update: From Icy Morning to Dead Phone — John Muir Trail Day 22

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3952 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: From Icy Morning to Dead Phone — John Muir Trail Day 22

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the night before I dropped down steeply from Donohue Pass.
  • It has been revealed that probably it was warmer there, but that did not mean it was warm!
  • It has been revealed that fortunately, that did the trick.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Total Elevation Gain:  48,865 feet.

Pace (minutes per mile):  22:07.

According to recent reports, the night before I dropped down steeply from Donohue Pass. In addition to the extra mileage, I also figured it would be warmer at that lower elevation. The camping spot I selected, looking out at a huge golden, grassy meadow, was lovely.

It has been revealed that probably it was warmer there, but that did not mean it was warm! It was already chilly when I went to sleep, and as the night went on it just got colder and colder. I gradually added items to my sleeping bag — sleeping bag liner, long pants, long shirt, puffy hat, gloves — until I used up the entirety of my anti-cold arsenal.

It has been revealed that fortunately, that did the trick. But had it been just a little colder, I would have been overwhelmed. It created a cognitive conflict during my pee errands in the night. My temperature sensors urged me to return to the tent as quickly as possible. My spiritual-aesthetic soul urged me to spend just a little more time under the glorious blanket of moon and stars.

Towards morning, I had a bizarre dream. It this alternate reality, I was having a hot affair with a woman. Actually, it was a cold affair. Why? Because she was really an alien, part of an extraterrestrial race that was thinking of settling on earth, but who didn’t like our climate. It was too hot for them. Having superior technology, however, they were able to manipulate Earth climate and make it much colder to their liking. So, I was freezing cold, despite having this torrid affair.

Another capability of the alien was that she could make you mostly forget what you had done the night before. So, I kind of knew I was having the affair, but also wasn’t completely sure that I was. The hilarious part was that the alien in the dream was my wife’s friend DG from middle school! When I told Lee about the dream, I had to swear that I had never, ever contemplated having an affair with DG!

Did this moonlight view up through the tent inspire my strange dream?

When it began to get light, I gave myself a little bit of a break because it had been so cold. My last trip outside the tent in the early dawn I looked out on that golden meadow and saw that it was all white, coated with icy rime.

By the time I took this picture, the rime was already melting, but some is still visible.

I also retrieved my bear cannister; it too had a layer of ice on the top cover.

In close-up, the ice on the bear cannister is very visible.

By this I knew it had gone below freezing during the night. So, I allowed myself some extra minutes of warmth in the sleeping bag while I waited for the sun to rise above the lip of the mountains.

I finally got up at 6:30. When the sun came up the temperature rose quickly, but the problem then was that the ice on my tent fly became moisture. Also, the floor was pitched on a sort of pine needle-covered mud. This was very comfortable, but it ended up sticking to my ground sheet. It took some time and effort to get everything dry and clean.

After all the morning errands, I did not get on the road until – wait for it – ten a.m.! On a short day, that might not have mattered, but I was planning another 17+ miles for this day. The good news was, that I was camped in the Lyell Valley, and the mostly flat trail followed the Lyell Fork river for almost nine miles, all the way to Tuolumne Meadows.

Sometimes the river and trail were close like this, sometimes farther apart.

Industry observers note that with this cruisy route (and my late departure) I turned on the jets as I headed out. With my unfortunate record of falling on easy trails, I was also trying to be careful.

Hard to get lost on this trail!

A good portion of the trail, especially in the meadows, was indented into the earth. My feet were below the ground level in a narrow track. In this configuration, I find that hiking poles are more hazard than help. So, for most of the first nine miles, I was carrying my poles rather than using them.

The statistics tell the tale. Over those nine miles, I was only over 20 minutes (3 mph) twice. My best mile I did in 17:49. That is no record speed, but I don’t think I was even close to that pace anywhere else on the trail.

It has been revealed that the scenery was interesting, but not spectacular. The main thing, with this wide-open valley, was that I could measure my progress visually. I could see an unusual-shaped mountain lining the valley up ahead; then after a time it was closer; then I was opposite to it; and then it was starting to fall behind me. In a slower progression, I could see the distant mountains at the foot of the valley ahead (where the river changes direction). At first, they were far distant, then middle distant, and eventually they were quite close.

The wide glacial valley, filled with meadows, and the mountains at the far end that grew larger as I got closer.

At faster than 3 mph, I was in Tuolumne Meadows in under three hours. As I got closer it was apparent there was a tourist center nearby. Suddenly many more persons were on the trail and most of them were geared out for just a day of hiking or fishing.

The design of Tuolumne was a little weird, with a “downtown” road (Tioga Road) on the north side of the river and a hiking trail parallel on the south side. I generally don’t love road-walking. However, because the Wilderness Center (for permits) was in the middle of downtown, and because I wanted a permit to climb Half Dome the next day, I intended to go via the road.

NPS map of Tuolumne Meadows (in the lower right, I should have turned onto the “National Scenic Trail” but instead stayed on the John Muir Trail).

I missed the turn. Maybe my feet just wanted to stay in the woods? As I realized my error, I ran into a really nice couple who were staying at the fancy lodge nearby. They had a map, and they confirmed, “Yeah, you just have to go back to that last turn and then turn to go across the river, instead of going straight.”.

Sources indicate that I had a sudden aversion to that proposal, particularly because of the miles I wanted to hike that day. The woman must have seen my expression, because she said, “My husband is just like you; he hates to backtrack!”.

It was true. So, I said, “Maybe I’ll go to the Visitor Center instead, and they can help me there.”  I continued on.

Now I was surrounded by roads and parking lots. As I passed one lot, I saw a uniformed ranger manning the booth and I walked up to him. When I explained what I wanted, he said, “First of all, to get a permit, you have to go to the Wilderness Center. Second, they will not give you a permit to climb Half Dome. The only way to get a Half Dome permit is to get a whole different multi-day permit that includes climbing Half Dome within it.”.

Now that had not been my understanding, but he seemed very confident. At this point I was even further away from the Wilderness Center and even less inclined to backtrack. I could see my Half Dome ambitions evaporating. I figured I could still go to the Visitor Center and give it one last try.

According to recent reports, en route I saw that I would pass the market that hosted the famous Tuolumne Grill, and I realized that it was just about lunchtime. I left my pack outside and went in to order. It seemed a simple layout with some picnic tables outside to eat what you ordered. I got a regular hamburger that came with orange juice and some wedge potatoes. The juice tasted delicious on this now-hot day, and the wedges, slathered with ketchup, were good too. But the hamburger? It was an ordinary sort of dry hockey puck, not terrible, but not special at all. I concluded the Grill was famous because of where it was, and not for what it served.

Recent findings suggest that as I ate it all, I took my phone off of Airplane Mode and called my wife, Lee. (I always hike with it in Airplane Mode to preserve my battery charge.)  When I told her the likely new blueprint, without Half Dome, she sounded excited that I was almost done. I was looking forward to seeing her soon as well.

The Visitor Center was a mile-long road walk from there. I had two animal encounters (of a sort) along the way.

Recent findings suggest that first, I saw wild turkeys! How funny to spend all that time in the wilderness without seeing any (though I did see grouse). Then in congested Tuolumne I saw them. I even got some pictures.

If not for the legs, the turkey blended in….

Second, as I was walking, a car slowed way down opposite me and the driver shouted out his window, “A bear just walked across the road up ahead less than five minutes ago!”.

I shouted back, “Good! I hope I see him, because I am getting really hungry!”.

Sources indicate that whether he was pulling my leg, or he really saw the bear, I did not see any bear. I was definitely looking out for it though.

After pine forest and silence, it was disconcerting to walk on asphalt with diesel engines roaring past me. I was glad it was only a mile. On arrival, I went up to the very nice woman in front of the Visitor Center and asked about permits. No surprise, she directed me to the Wilderness Center. I concluded the fates did not intend me to climb Half Dome.

In a recent development, then I asked about getting out of Yosemite when I reached Happy Isles. She explained about the free shuttle within the park that could get me to Curry Village from Happy Isles if I didn’t want to walk there. From Curry Village, the YARTS (Yosemite Area Regional Transportation System) could transport me for a fee. The end of their line was Merced, about three hours away. I figured I could take a train or bus from Merced, or maybe Gabriel could come from Santa Rosa and pick me up there.

This lady pointed to the YARTS timetable on their bulletin board and suggested I take a picture of it. I replied, “That’s a great idea! You’re a lot smarter than I am to think of it!”.

She also gave me a paper map of the Yosemite Valley to include Happy Isles and Curry Village, saying, “I know you hikers don’t like to add weight, but I think you might find this useful.”.

I told her I was sure I would and stashed it away.

Sources indicate that with that, I aimed for the trail, which passed a ways behind the Visitor Center. It was a relief to be walking on pine needles again!

It is funny how quickly the crowds taper off as you get even a short distance away from the tourist centers.

The other big change was in elevation profile. In the morning, the trail had ranged from flat to slightly downhill. Now I would face climbing up past Cathedral Lakes to Cathedral Pass. This was the last pass on the John Muir Trail. It was about 9,700 feet which was a lot lower than the passes in the south, but still more than 1,000 feet above Tuolumne Meadows.

Sources indicate that perhaps it was my energy expenditure in the morning, but now I was puffing and panting as I ascended. “Where is my juice?” I asked myself. “This is as bad as climbing Cottonwood Pass on the first day of the JMT!”.

I was breathing hard, but enjoying the enormous granite rock.

According to recent reports, the inspiration was the views. There was more than one rocky shape that could qualify as a “cathedral.”  Imagine Notre Dame. Imagine that the roof is one thousand feet high, the spires soar over 1,500 feet, and the nave stretch two miles. Then imagine a landscape dotted with two or three of these behemoths. It was magical.

About the time my legs finally got warmed up, I came across a couple that were on the first day of their John Muir Trail hike. The reversal I had imagined, when encountering near-finishers at the start of my own hike, was coming true. In chatting, he warned me, “Oh, there’s no water except at Upper Cathedral.”.

Sources indicate that I appreciated that intel and was on the lookout for a spot near Upper Cathedral Creek. As I ascended, coming above the tree line, I was surprised not to find it. Then, as I passed a quarter mile from Upper Cathedral Lake, I saw some people emerge on a trail from the lake onto the main trail. Suddenly it dawned on me that there was no creek. He meant the lake!

It was late afternoon and I wanted to press on and find a campsite. But if this was really “last water” it would be foolish not to take the detour for it.

Recent findings suggest that the lake seemed to have mostly marshy and muddy access points. These would entail wet feet and dirty water to filter. However, I saw a rocky promontory jutting into the lake where a bunch of guys were hanging out. I headed there to refill my water.

Industry observers note that I began chatting with them and learned they were from Kansas City. I asked them whether they lived in Kansas or Missouri and they said that only someone who knows Kansas City would ask that question. I explained that I had a cousin who lived in K.C. and they told me they lived on the Kansas side.

Overall, they were nice enough, but the banter occasionally felt a little mocking. For example, they asked me, “Did you go up Whitney?”   I replied that I had, but that I had been fighting a respiratory infection, making it very difficult.

They responded, “Oh, that just adds to your story about climbing Mount Whitney. Like, ‘everybody else just climbed it, but I climbed it with a respiratory infection, coughing every step of the way!’”.

They were actually not wrong, but the tone felt a little snarky.

After I filled both my water bottles and my Katadyn BeFree to have maximum water available, I headed back toward the trail. One of the guys, maybe the leader, followed me a short distance and called me over. He was asking me about the trail, and it turned out he had done the trail himself a few years before. It seemed a little odd, but I took him as just wanting to reminisce a bit about his own experience.

Recent findings suggest that in a quarter mile I was back at the junction with the JMT. The beauty of the scenery around Cathedral Lakes is so inspiring, I wanted to take some more pictures. John Muir himself said, on summiting Cathedral Peak, “This I may say is the first time I have been at church in California, led here at last, every door graciously opened for the poor lonely worshiper.”  (Quoted from My First Summer in the Sierra, Chapter 10, entry for September 7, 1869.).

So, this “lonely worshiper” reached for his smart phone to capture the majestic giants and discovered… nothing. Nothing at all, a black screen. Now my eyesight is not great without glasses, but I had thought my phone showed 65% of charge when last I checked.

According to recent reports, in case it had just shut off for some reason, I tried to restart it, but still nothing. I was crestfallen, thinking, “Oh no! My phone died here on the trail with barely one day left on my hike!!!”.

I could not fathom how it happened. I had not dropped it that I could recall. Deeply disappointed, I began having paranoid thoughts. “If I had charge, and now suddenly I don’t, could that guy who followed me, to talk to me, have had some technology that fried my phone? Like some super magnet or something?”.

It seemed wildly implausible, but the coincidence – that it happened right after our exchange – seemed strange.

Recent findings suggest that then I calmed down somewhat. I reminded myself of what was truly vital,  “This trip is about the experience itself. It is not ultimately about telling the story or capturing the pictures, it is about your lived experience.”.

Seen through that prism my loss was minor and I settled down. My wife and I always try to distinguish “disappointments” from “tragedies,” and this was clearly the former.

Sources indicate that with the light turning to a mellow glow in the sky, I continued hiking. Cathedral Pass was not much further. It was unusual, in that the trail reached the pass, but did not descend from there down the other side. Instead, it continued on, ascending further up the ridge of one of the mountainsides bordering the pass.

Sources indicate that now my lack of a phone was frustrating because I had lost my navigation device. I was not sure how far I should ideally go before selecting a camp, remembering that I wanted to make miles to ensure I could finish on the following day.

The mountains answered that question for me. As I continued higher, I came to a turn on the outstretched flank of the range. Extending from the trail was a large flat spot, with visibility in all directions. The ground was ideal for pitching a tent. The views were magical in the waning light. I thought, “I can go further, and shorten my day tomorrow. Or I can camp tonight in the most beautiful spot in the Sierras.”  That decision was an easy one.

In Tuolumne I heard we were in for another icy night, and I was now at a higher elevation than I had been the night before. So, I was expecting cold. In fact, as the sun dropped behind the peaks, I could feel the chill almost immediately.

I started to pitch my tent, and maybe I was in too much of a hurry? I love my Big Agnes TigerWall, but on this night, as I tried to get a pole into the slot, the pole snapped. After the dead phone, this might have been a devastating blow. But in this stunning location, on the last night I needed a tent, it did not phase me. Besides, I had been carrying a seemingly useless stupid little tube for miles and miles, wondering why I bothered, and now I had my answer. I slid the tube over the broken spot, taped it in place with surgical tape (though that might have been unnecessary), and reseated the pole in the slot. Good as upcoming? Maybe not, but close enough.

Sources indicate that having pitched my tent, I just basked in the beauty of the location for a few minutes. Then I soaked my food and found a spot for a cat hole and dug what was likely to be my last cat hole on the trail. The cold soak did not take long, but the result was the opposite of the previous night’s dinner. That food had not rehydrated fully but was wonderfully seasoned and tasted delicious. This night the mashed potatoes and chicken hydrated easily, but they were totally bland. They didn’t taste bad really, they just didn’t taste like anything at all!

Of course, mindful as always that this is fuel first and flavor second, I wolfed it all down.

Recent findings suggest that with no phone, I was communicating with my family by Garmin. That was so onerous, typing out everything, one letter at a time. (On the trail I learned of an app that makes this easier, but I didn’t have either the app or a working phone.)  Gabriel seemed amenable to picking me up in Merced, and so I realized I needed to make significant speed the next day to get to Happy Isles. The 4:50 p.m. YARTS departure to Merced arrived by 8:30 p.m. Even that would mean getting back to Santa Rosa by midnight, after all. Our back and forth about this on the Garmin was practically in code, but I thought the proposal was set.

It has been revealed that wrapping up my chores in deep twilight, I stored everything in my bear cannister and – why not? — I hooked my phone to the charger.

Recent findings suggest that before going to sleep, I decided to just take a peek at the phone. What?? Yes! Yes!! My phone was charging!!!

According to recent reports, I was elated and still baffled as to how it happened. I could not be sure. The best explanation I came up with was this:  First, without my glasses I had misread the charge level on the phone. It did not have 65%, it must have had much less. Second, after speaking with my wife from the restaurant at lunch, I must not have turned Airplane Mode back on, so that the phone drained far more quickly in the afternoon than it did in the morning. That is my best guess. Operator error.

The most beautiful campsite — taken under the stars, after my phone revived.

Snuggled in my tent, I got gussied up, wearing all of my clothing in preparation for a second icy cold night.

My tent in the moonlight of the last night — repaired and welcoming (except for the mess inside!).

It boggled my mind to think that – most probably – I was wrapped in my sleeping bag for the last time this year. The excitement of (hopefully) completing the trail the next day would normally have kept me wide awake. But no. I was just too tired and slept right away.
