⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The seven-person panel that constitutes Idaho’s Fish and Game Commission is down to six after commissioner Brody Harshbarger resigned Wednesday amid pressure from sportsmen and at least one state lawmaker.
  • It has been revealed that “Your service on the commission is concluded, effective immediately,” wrote Gov.
  • Industry observers note that harshbarger was charged in March with seven wildlife violations from the 2025 hunting season, including poaching two bull elk in Fremont County, where he lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The seven-person panel that constitutes Idaho’s Fish and Game Commission is down to six after commissioner Brody Harshbarger resigned Wednesday amid pressure from sportsmen and at least one state lawmaker. Harshbarger took a plea deal on Nov. 9 to dismiss five of seven charges related to illegally killing two bull elk in the region he represents.

It has been revealed that “Your service on the commission is concluded, effective immediately,” wrote Gov. Brad Little’s chief of staff, Zach Hauge, in response to Harshbarger’s resignation, obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun. “Maintaining the integrity, credibility and effective operation of the Idaho Fish and Game Commission remains a top priority for Gov. Little.”.

Industry observers note that harshbarger was charged in March with seven wildlife violations from the 2025 hunting season, including poaching two bull elk in Fremont County, where he lives. The former commissioner stepped away from commission duties once he was charged, but retained his seat until this week while the case continued, effectively leaving the position vacant.

Related: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Charged with Poaching Elk, Trespassing, Says He’ll ‘Voluntarily Postpone’ Duties.

In a recent development, “I understand everyone deserves their day in court, but commissioners are charged with making and upholding our regulations,” Nick Fasciano, executive director of the Idaho Wildlife Federation, tells Outdoor Life. “And we do expect them to be held to a higher standard. The whole thing is disappointing.”.

The commission sets statewide hunting, fishing, and trapping seasons plus bag limits and other regulations based on recommendations and research supplied by Idaho Department of Fish and Game scientists. Each member of the commission can serve two four-year terms, and no more than four commissioners can come from the same political party. Harshbarger is a farmer in Ashton, Idaho. It’s an area known for massive chunks of public land and substantial grain and potato operations.

It has been revealed that “I love our wildlife and the community we live in,” Harshbarger’s profile read on the commission’s website before it was removed. “We have a lot of challenges, and I am excited to help continue to solve them. What an amazing place to live and work.”.

Harshbarger pled guilty to hunting without a tag and shooting across a road. The remaining five charges, which are being dismissed in exchange for his guilty plea, are two illegal big-game kills, hunting from a vehicle, failure to retrieve game, and trespass (one bull was on private property).

When news of Harshbarger’s plea deal went public, hunters and anglers started contacting regional IDFG offices and the governor’s office to demand his removal. The plea deal means his penalties could be as low as $500 and a one-year hunting suspension when he’s sentenced Dec. 9.

Frustration has also boiled over on social media around Harshbarger’s case.

“Wake up Governor Little and do the right thing,” one Instagram user commented on the news of the plea deal, prior to Harshbarger’s resignation. “You and Senator Risch are already working to sell off our public lands and now you won’t step in to protect our wild game. Shame on you two.”.

Harshbarger was appointed by Gov. Little in 2024.

In a recent development, “Public trust is difficult to earn and easily lost,” wrote Idaho state Rep. David Leavitt in an email sent to Little on Tuesday that called for Harshbarger’s dismissal. “Maintaining that trust requires us to uphold the same principles regardless of who is involved. Idaho citizens deserve nothing less.”.

Little is also now in charge of appointing the director of IDFG. The commission did that until this year, when Little signed a publicly opposed bill into law changing the procedure from a seven-person decision to a one-person appointment by the governor, with confirmation by the state Senate.

According to recent reports, “Commissioners and the director now serve at the pleasure of the governor,” Fasciano states. “The commission is not empowered to boot out one of their own members even if they were so inclined.”.

Current IDFG director Jim Fredericks, a career fisheries biologist, was already leading the agency when the new law took effect July 1, making him the state’s last director selected by the commission.

Read Next: Montana Man Banned from Hunting for 20 Years After Bowhunters Watch Him Poach a Trophy Bull.

It has been revealed that “The actual department of Fish and Game is going to take some heat for this [Harshbarger incident], but they weren’t the decision makers here,” Fasciano says. “The commission and the director were not able to drive a resolution here and they are also not responsible for the sentencing. A lot of frustration is going to be directed toward them, that isn’t their fault.”.

Excerpted from the novel Nearshore (Viking, 2026).

Palmer was midspan on the Tunitas Creek Bridge, southbound, when the boat came into view through the gunsight notch of the arroyo. It was a Whaler circling clockwise fast and tight, maybe a quarter mile beyond the surf.

It has been revealed that he’d wanted to ride a few waves at a sandbar that had been assembling itself over the past few days at Pomponio. A quick lunch-break session before the wind came up. But then he got the call about the boat, and now that he saw it spinning he also saw that his day was officially fucked. He crossed the bridge and powered up the Coast Highway to the overlook at the top of the rise. He lifted his Bushnells from the dashboard and got out of the truck and glassed the vessel.

The wake’s widening spiral told him the wheel had been hard to starboard a good long while. It looked to be stirring up some kind of suicidal whirlpool.

#79568. 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1524 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred.
  • Despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried.
  • Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no plans for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

Despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no plans for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

After landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

On the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

In a recent development, however, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

We did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

According to recent reports, linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden noted, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”.

Linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

Survival promptly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

Sources indicate that one of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling blueprint was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden remarked. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”.

Assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other prepares. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

Recent findings suggest that next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden stated. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”.

Industry observers note that pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden said, “the final lap or two is about racing.”.

According to recent reports, when things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

According to recent reports, her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden mentioned. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”.

Recent findings suggest that while Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden stated. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”.

#79567. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Deer Like a Real Woodsman

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2451 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Deer Like a Real Woodsman

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2451 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the major whitetail buck and I badly startled each other.
  • After the rifle’s roar shattered the forest stillness, I heard a couple more rhythmic thumps as the by-now invisible deer continued bounding.
  • But then came a distant, wood-splintering racket, followed by silence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the major whitetail buck and I badly startled each other. In the steady rain patter, he apparently didn’t hear me until I’d stillhunted very close to his cedar clump shelter. I almost came unglued when he exploded into view, too spooked to even snort.

After the rifle’s roar shattered the forest stillness, I heard a couple more rhythmic thumps as the by-now invisible deer continued bounding. So much for my semi-frantic snapshot.

But then came a distant, wood-splintering racket, followed by silence. Without snow, it took awhile to slowly, alertly follow up. I found the heart-shot buck. That terminal crash noise came from his failing to clear a windfall when the carburetor quit for keeps.

Industry observers note that that’s stillhunting at its best. Unlike the prolonged tedium of trail watching or waiting out a drive, stillhunting’s uptight anticipation is an ongoing thrill. When the action does come, it’s often sudden, without warning. Don’t hunt this way if you have a weak heart.

Sources indicate that very old-timers like my 87-year-old father tell me that forest stillhunting was far more common decades ago. Maybe today’s urban hunters don’t trust their stealth and woodcraft skills. Although not an easy way to take woodland game, including elk, the bottom-line reality is that stillhunting can produce game when other tactics cannot.

Obviously, a lone-wolf hunter can’t make drives to himself. Even when sufficient manpower is available, effective drives require thorough knowledge of both the terrain and how local deer use it. If game chooses not to move because it fed well last night, lacks sexual ambition just now or doesn’t like the prevailing weather, trail watching is usually hopeless. For that matter, many mule deer and most elk and moose simply don’t stick that much to established trails.

The stillhunter is free of such vagaries. Instead of hoping game will come to him, he goes to it — although stillhunting is not the stalking of game already located. Tactically, he has two top priorities. First, to move quietly and alertly, his course basically dictated by wind, terrain and possibly sun direction. Second, to discover game before it sees, hears or smells him. The stillhunter must play a lone-hand game — two hunters seem to make not twice, but four times the noise of one hunter.

Recent findings suggest that slow movement is a must. A stillhunter covering ground too swiftly simply can’t look well enough for concealed game. He also can’t help making extra noise to be picked up by critters who depend on acute hearing every day of their lives to stay out of trouble. They easily detect high frequency noises (including any rustles, squeaks or metallic clinks from our gear and garb) that we often can’t hear.

Industry observers note that the real trick in stillhunting is to do the looking and the moving as two separate functions. If you forget everything else, remember that! When you attempt to look for game and move your feet at the same time, sooner or later you will make unwanted noise — snapping a brittle twig, tripping noisily or whatever.

According to recent reports, don’t follow any set rhythm of taking a set number of steps, then stopping. Instead, consider the area that you can see from where you stand as one vision zone. I never move until this zone, of up to 180° ahead and to both sides, has been totally studied.

A vision zone may range out only 50 feet in dense woods or 200-plus yards in more open country. Depending on the extent of the zone, terrain and cover, it may take 30 seconds or several minutes of methodical looking. Often a promising area is worth the time to just sit for extra eyeballing.

Don’t expect to see a full-blown deer or elk looming up ahead like calendar artwork. Look for just parts of the animal as clues. Most forest visuals are vertical lines — tree trunks, etc. An out-of-place horizontal line may be a log or the outline of a deer’s back. A smudge of dull yellow may be autumn leaves or an elk rump. Wide-field binoculars help greatly on such details.

Once, while hunting in the Cascade Mountains, my eye caught a tiny movement ahead. A broad leaf twitching with the breeze? But there was no breeze and, in that evergreen thicket, no deciduous leaves. I waited some minutes, then spotted the movement again for what it was — a blacktail doe’s ear twitching as its owner listened. When she finally moved, right behind her came a shootable buck.

After searching a visual zone (and listening, too), select a route for the next few feet or yards, based on avoidance of brush contact or other potential noise. Footwork is crucial. Short steps are quietest. They offer best control of shifting your balance if you ease your foot down and feel a twig likely to snap under full weight. Also, only with short steps can you come down slowly and silently on your toes or the ball of your foot. Long steps force the heel down first, making it much more likely that you will snap twigs or make a soft but tell-tale thud.

Recent findings suggest that want some expert stillhunting lessons? Simply watch a house cat on the prowl for birds or field mice. Slow movement, long look-listen pauses, obvious patience and great concentration are what make felines the finest stillhunters in nature. Once, in Washington’s mountains, I watched a mountain lion on the prowl. This best-of-all deer hunter resembles a magnified house cat at work.

Big or small, hunting cats are superb at using concealment. You should do likewise. Very often, unseen game ahead will hear you. By moving slowly with minimum noise, you may sound much like just another deer. But the listening quarry will be watching in your direction for visual confirmation. Don’t slow yourself any more than necessary. I use camouflage makeup to make my pale face less visible against dark forest backdrop.

Industry observers note that if you can move quietly in some kind of concealment, use that route rather than an easier-looking, more open course. Stick to shadows; avoid sunlit patches. When possible, hunt with the sun behind you. Go over ridgetops with caution, using brush or timber cover. If the hilltop lacks cover, try crawling. Of course, stillhunting must be done into the wind or at least across it — never downwind. Although human sense of smell is pretty pathetic, sometimes the barnyard odor of elk ahead can be detected.

According to recent reports, often a stillhunter has the option of following fresh game tracks. Except under ideal conditions, such as fresh snow, one-man tracking demands so much attention that the stillhunter is distracted while he should be looking for actual game. More than once, deer or elk have surprised me, costing me a shot simply because I was distracted by some interesting tracks. If you start trailing, remember that the maker of these tracks may be bedded down somewhere ahead and almost certainly watching his backtrail. To get anywhere close to it will require extremely good stillhunting.

Industry observers note that the lay of the land can be friend or foe. Ridges and hills offer chances to surprise game on the other side. Flat country is tougher because it offers few elevation advantages to the hunter. Although knowing the area always helps, it’s not truly essential for stillhunting. Once, a young stillhunter in our party, newly introduced to the place, nailed a whitetail buck the second morning. A fast learner, he capped that next year by pussyfooting close enough to a Cascades bull elk to take him with a bow.

According to recent reports, the inexperienced stillhunter is often tempted to work mature evergreen timber, where dense shade means little underbrush. But closely spaced conifers self-prune their branches profusely, forming a noisy layer of dead twigs. Such forests can be hunted only when there’s enough wind noise to cover the hunter’s snap-crackle-pop progress. Unless soggy from rain or wet snow, dead leaves are another audio booby trap.

Industry observers note that some timber is open enough to have a good growth of clover or grass, particularly attractive to elk. By contrast, dense coniferous forests contain little ground-level browse to attract feeding game, but they often provide good escape cover when hunting pressure is on. In unseasonably warm weather, the cool shade of thick evergreen timber invites game. In cold weather, the evergreen canopy traps radiant ground heat for considerably warmer bedding than more open forests.

Where evergreen timber is lacking, game makes the best of thick brushy cover or tall grasses — the latter is commonly a deer favorite. In real cold or after rain, any warming sun draws game to south or west-facing slopes.

Best time of day for stillhunting depends on several factors. Stillhunting as early as light permits may find game feeding or on the move to bedding. Ground litter then is less noisy, thanks to the night’s dampening dew. But if overnight frost has made fallen leaves ultra-brittle or has crusted the snow, better wait for some midday thawing.

Industry observers note that though rain or a moderate wind helps mask hunter movement sounds, strong winds are a mixed blessing. With their hearing impaired by too much wind, restless animals change location often rather than staying put. That aids the stillhunter, because moving game is far easier to see. But wind-jittery animals, up on their feet and watching for danger they can’t hear, can spot the hunter more readily. Fortunately, a stiff wind covers his extra noise if the stillhunter sticks to thicker cover for extra concealment.

Worst of all are those dead-calm Indian summer days, when even your shadow seems to make a racket in the dried-out forest. The only option, then, is to hunt terrain where game can be spotted at a considerable distance (example: from one ridge to another).

In a recent development, some cover simply can’t be stillhunted. Swampy terrain is impossibly noisy, all the more if there’s any ice to be broken. Dry, fluffy snow can be fairly quiet for walking. But typical autumn snow, heavy and wet, is composed of oversize, many-pointed flakes. Each step compression-shatters untold thousands of such crystalline flakes. That accounts for the appallingly loud squeakiness. Until it’s settled, breaking its flakes in the process, such snow is no good for stillhunting. The settling process may take two or three days unless a thaw speeds it.

Sources indicate that snow characteristics may vary with terrain. North-facing snow is little affected by the weak sun of late autumn, but snow on southern and western slopes settles rapidly with a few hours of sun.

Industry observers note that the stillhunter must remember that weather affects game’s likely location. The first serious snowfall often causes deer to hole up in the shelter of thick, low-branching evergreens, where they may stay 48 to 72 hours, believe it or not, even during the rut. Hungry when they finally leave cover, deer then are likely to feed during the day. But until they start moving, the pristine snow will be barren of tracks, leading to the false conclusion that all game has moved out.

Of course, game does move out of high country when substantial snowstorms hit. Hunting deer and elk on such vertical migration routes is often considered a trail-watching game. The stillhunter can cover more territory to learn where game is moving — and if it’s moving.

Industry observers note that gear and clothing are critical in stillhunting. Soft leather boots with crepe soles are almost moccasin-quiet but treacherous in steep, wet or rocky terrain. Classic, Maine-style, rubber shoepacs make quiet steps. Their rounded sole edges are not as likely to shear-snap noisy twigs as stiffer, sharp-edged soles do. With any other rubber footwear, wear enough socks to prevent empty space around the foot from audibly pumping air at each step.

In a recent development, harder, composition soles with lugs are necessary to maintain life and limb in rough country. Alas, such footwear is noisier. The only consolation is that in country steep enough to require lug-soled boots, the stillhunter has a longer “working range” across canyons, etc., and is not quite as vulnerable to making noise as the close-range, flatland hunter. At times, I’ve carried soft sneakers in my daypack to slip on after climbing a ridge that demanded lug-soled, ankle-supportive boots. Another useful trick is to wear a pair of knit leg warmers running from knee-height to ankles. These muffle twig noise and grass swish.

Clothing choice is very simple. Whatever the material, it must be soft. Nylon, corduroy and stiff denim are too noisy. Wool and flannel are the great favorites for quiet movement. Some synthetics like orlon and acrylic are almost as good, depending on weave and nap. Rubberized raingear makes less noise than nylon or vinyl. Because a hat’s brim snags noisy branches, wear a cap. Again, wool or knitted acrylic is quietest. I made a simple, woolen pack cover to keep my backpack from imitating a snare drum when I hunker through overhanging branches.

In a recent development, for quiet carrying, a firearm’s barrel length is more critical than weight per se. Although carbines are best, one of my favorite woods rifles has a 24-inch barrel. I find a 26-inch barrel is just too easy to bang against branches. A timber riflescope should have at least a 30-foot field at 100 yards — more would be better, because forest shots are often at close-range game on the run. Yellow shooting glasses contrast brown deer and elk better against evergreen backgrounds.

Pocket hardware like keys, coins and cartridges must be handkerchief-wrapped to eliminate tell-tale clinking. When I rendezvoused with my deer-hunting daughter in the woods, her sardonic greeting was, “Hello, Santa!”.

“Well before I saw you,” she continued, “I could hear you playing ‘Jingle Bells’. What’s in your pockets?”.

Sources indicate that A ring of unwrapped keys, that’s what. And deer probably could hear it twice as well as she could.

Although usually not physically taxing, stillhunting is tiring if you do it right. What wears you out is the strain of constant vigilance. And I mean constant! About the time you relax or daydream, up bounds a buck or bull that makes good his escape because you weren’t mentally prepared to react quite fast enough. But if you’re a dedicated hunter, the high-tension hours of stillhunting are memorable whether you score or not.

Latest Update: How to Call Ducks: A Beginner’s Guide

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • In a recent development, if you’re reading this, you probably suck at calling ducks.
  • So why learn how to call ducks at all?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

In a recent development, if you’re reading this, you probably suck at calling ducks. Don’t feel insulted, though, because most people suck at calling ducks. Nash Buckingham once wrote, “A duck call in the hands of a novice is one of the greatest conservation tools known to man.” Maybe that’s not entirely true, but you could shoot a lifetime’s worth of ducks without ever learning how to call ducks, or even owning a duck call.

So why learn how to call ducks at all? Well, good calling absolutely does work under certain circumstances, and because of that, it will result in more ducks in the bag for you. It’s also an enjoyable part of the waterfowling experience. So, here’s everything you need to know to learn how to call ducks—and ultimately become a better duck hunter.

It has been revealed that there are some 30 huntable duck species in North America, but most duck hunters rely exclusively on the sounds of the hen mallard when they’re duck calling. There are several reasons for that. Mallards are far and away the most common and most hunted duck species, and they’re one of the most responsive to calling. Mallard hens are also loud and vocal, and since they frequently mix with other dabbling duck species, their calls sound natural to all of them. Also, it’s just tradition. Though live ducks do far more whistling and peeping than quacking, folks still look at you weird if you whistle too much in the blind, as if you’re a grown man eating Skittles or something. So, the standard-issue duck call is designed to imitate the sounds of a Suzie, which is the universal nickname for a hen mallard. So, henceforth, when I generically say “duck call,” I’m referring to a hen mallard call.

In a recent development, duck calls vary slightly in design, materials, and price, but they all share the same basic components, including a barrel, end piece, and reeds. J-frame calls are easier to disassemble, clean, and reassemble without affecting the sound. Louisiana-style calls provide wider tuning versatility.

Industry observers note that most calls have either one reed or two; single reeds tend to be higher-pitched and louder, so they’re generally favored by open-water and field hunters. Double-reed calls are often softer in pitch and easier to blow with less air, making them a favorite for close quarters.

Recent findings suggest that duck calls are generally made of acrylic, polycarbonate, or wood. Acrylic calls are the most expensive, but they sound great and are easy to maintain. They provide loud, crisp sounds in the hands of a good caller. Polycarbonate calls are essentially plastic and can provide volume comparable to acrylic calls. Some say they’re not quite as realistic; I say you and the ducks won’t hear the difference. An acrylic call looks better, but for most hunters, it won’t provide any better service than a polycarbonate one. Wooden calls look better than both, and they tend to produce a softer sound that’s ideal for close-in calling. But because moisture can cause the wood to swell, and because there’s a lot of moisture in duck hunting, wooden calls do require more maintenance.

A good caller can make any duck call sound good, but the best, most expensive call will not help a terrible caller. Learn the basics on something inexpensive, and then, if you want to invest in a high-quality call, try several to see which suits you best.

Mallards have a wide vocabulary, but there are only a handful of calls a hunter needs to master, including the basic quack, the greeting call, the comeback call, and the chuckle (variations of this last sound can replicate both excited ducks flying in the air as well as ducks feeding on the water). It is a pure waste of words for me to attempt to describe what each of these calls sounds like when there are good YouTube videos. So here are some YouTube videos.

New callers usually struggle with two things that make their sounds sub-par: improper air pressure and the wrong cadence. Veteran callers will advise newbies to “blow from their chest.” To get the reeds of a duck call to “break” into the proper rasp, you need deep air pressure huffed from the diaphragm. It’s almost like retching or hiccupping, but not as unpleasant. Finding that air pressure isn’t difficult, but it does require practice. Different calls require varying amounts of air pressure, too, to get just the right ducky sound. You’ll know it when you hear it.

It has been revealed that the right cadence is even more crucial. Hens make various calls with varying degrees of excitement, but the notes will be crisp and consistent. Slurred-together quacking is the No. 1 dead giveaway of a terrible duck caller. You don’t want everyone else in the marsh to hear that.

Remember those 29 or so other duck species I mentioned? They all make sounds, and you should make some of them, too, even if your buddies look at you funny in the blind. Blue-winged teal are especially vocal ducks, but gadwalls, pintails, wigeon, and wood ducks can all be duped with the right sounds. Drake mallards make a distinct call that’s a blend of a nasally quack and whistle, and it is absolutely unmistakable. Even divers, like canvasbacks and bluebills, make a soft growling sound that can be replicated with a regular call and can sometimes get their attention.

Industry observers note that the hens of many dabbling species make shrill quacks, while drakes make softer peeps and whistles. You can replicate sounds like blue-winged teal hen quacks and drake gadwall gnack-gnacks on your regular duck call, and use a duck whistle to make sounds like drake green-winged teal peeps, pintail and wigeon whistles, and mallard drake gweebs. Companies like Haydel’s Game Calls also make a variety of “other species” calls, including diver calls and wood duck whistles.

These subtle sounds are more than just support for quacking. Big flocks of real ducks make a lot of noise, and having a spread of decoys that don’t whistle actually sounds fairly unnatural. Besides that, whistles can be heard from a surprisingly long way, and they’re frequently more effective at turning flocks of “other” ducks than hen mallard calls.

In a recent development, the most important part of duck calling is not contest-stage calling perfection. Once you can make basic mallard sounds, supplemented by a few whistles and grunts, the key is watching how ducks react to your sounds and adjusting accordingly. Veteran waterfowlers call it “reading ducks,” and the hunter who makes a passable sound at the perfect time will call in more birds than the one who hits a perfect note at the wrong time.

It has been revealed that but unlike turkeys, which give unmistakable cues to your calling like gobbling and strutting, ducks respond with cues that are both more subtle and difficult to see since, you know, they’re flying in the sky. The most basic advice is to only call at wing-tips and tails; that is, don’t call at ducks that are flying toward you. Shut up and let them come, and save the calling for when they’re circling or flying away.

Yet, there are times when ducks that are looking right at you seem to prefer aggressive calling. I remember one morning in North Dakota years ago when we were turning distant flocks with urgent pintail whistles, and they wanted to hear those whistles until they were fully committed to the decoys and within gun range. On that same trip, but on a different day, we shot greenheads at tennis-racket distance over a pothole. Those ducks didn’t want to hear a call at all.

Industry observers note that duck moods change by the day, and the best callers “read the room” and adapt quickly. Let the first flock or two work your spread on their own, and if you get to shoot them without calling, take a hint. But if a few flocks pass over without so much as a look, hit them with a greeting call. If they circle but don’t commit, add in some quacks and feeding chatter. If a hen mallard gets excited and answers you in the air, pour it on thick and get her talking. Focus on talking to the ducks, not on showing your buddies how well you can call, and you will have mastered the most difficult part of calling ducks.

It has been revealed that A live hen mallard answering your calls is all the affirmation you need that your calls sound good. But that doesn’t happen on every hunt. Upcoming callers, and even experienced callers who are out of practice in the off-season, can always benefit by listening to live ducks. Wildlife refuges all over the country have observation areas where hunting is off-limits, but you can listen to relaxed ducks doing their thing. Even the semi-tame mallards at the city park can teach you a lot (plus you can confuse the city folk doing yoga by whipping out your duck call and practicing).

See a video of live ducks making quacks and greeting calls.

Sources indicate that youTube is also an outstanding resource, not only for bookmarking videos on how to reassemble an original Ruger Mark II or outboard motor starters, but also for listening to recordings of live critters, including ducks. So, if you really want to learn how to call ducks and get really good at it. Sit and listen to those videos, then practice some calling. Record yourself, play it back, and adjust your air pressure and cadence accordingly. So long as nobody’s watching, you can snack on Skittles, too.

The first thing you notice in an abandoned Spanish village is the swallows.

Industry observers note that outside, they swoop zestfully up and down in wavy crests and troughs, cutting through the air, darting through broken windows and front doors at reckless speed, slipping through holes in the masonry with astonishing precision, and alighting, casually, in their chosen nests. It’s as if they know every corner of the building. It’s as if they own the place.

And they do. There’s no one else here. By some estimates, Spain has more than three thousand abandoned villages. I was in one called Las Casillas de Bezas, in the eastern half of the country, in the province of Teruel, high-stepping over brambles, ducking as swallows darted around my head, and wondering if I was striding into the ancient past or the deep future.

I was on the trail of abandonment, particularly what follows when humans leave the countryside, which is happening not just in Spain, but across Europe, and.

For the skier who appreciates good design as much as good snow, these are a timeless gift. —Sierra Shafer, Editorial Director, Lifestyle.

Sources indicate that A cold beer after skiing is one of life’s simple pleasures. Cold fingers holding that beer? Less so. KAVU’s delightfully superfluous solution is a fleece mitten with a built-in pocket for your drink. Yes, it’s essentially a koozie for your hand and your beverage, and frankly, I wish I’d thought of it first. Is it necessary? Absolutely not, which is why it makes a great gift for your favorite parking-lot après regular. —SS.

Celebrating a ski day by dipping bread into melted cheese is an elite, unbeatable experience, but you don’t have to travel to the Alps to indulge. Le Creuset’s Alpine Signature Fondue Set brings the ritual right to your kitchen table. The enameled cast-iron pot retains heat beautifully, while six color-coded forks help everyone keep track of their bread. It’s a splurge, but it’s also the kind of gift that will become a tradition for years to come. As for the best recipe? My friend JF, an expert skier and even more accomplished fondue enthusiast, has entire books on the subject. His advice, which I’ll pass along as my holiday gift to you: Rub the inside of the pot with a cut garlic clove before adding the ingredients, use a combination of Gruyère and Emmentaler, and finish with a pinch of nutmeg. Whatever the recipe, double it. —SS.

I own several Rumpl blankets and use them year-round. Think of them as your favorite insulated jacket, only major enough to share. At parking-lot après, nothing beats throwing one over your lap in a camp chair. They’re just as useful wrapped around your shoulders while you cheer on your U12 racer bashing through slalom gates in subzero temps. A built-in clip keeps the blanket in place, leaving your hands free for whatever libations or cowbells the occasion calls for. I keep one in my car all winter, partly for emergencies but mostly because there’s always a reason to pull it out. With recycled synthetic insulation and a water-resistant shell, it’s warm, packable and endlessly useful. And yes, I’m suggesting you gift yourself one. Ho, ho, ho. —SS.

Industry observers note that hygge meets performance in this cozy fleece that doubles as an ultra-plush midlayer. We love the longer, relaxed cut that covers your backside, and the high, fuzzy collar is pure comfort when the snow starts swirling. The recycled pebbled pile is warm, quick-drying and moisture-wicking under a shell, though it’s so plush it’s almost overkill for skiing. Where it really shines is après and around town, thanks to fun prints in three colorways and men’s and women’s cuts. —Jenny Wiegand, Associate Gear Director.

Long winter nights call for warm pajamas. Hanna Andersson’s flannel PJ pants are so cozy you’ll want to wear them under your snow pants. They come in several ski-chic patterns that look good on the whole family, and they’re perfect for skiers who want something soft to climb into before dreaming of powder all night. —Giorgia Menetre, Senior Social Media Strategist.

Nothing beats taking off your ski boots and slipping into cozy slippers. If you’re like me, you want a pair that lasts, has a solid sole and isn’t the same old tan suede. L.L.Bean’s Daybreak slippers check every box. The wool clog-style upper keeps toes warm, the slip-on design makes them easy to pull on and off, and the durable rubber sole offers just enough traction. They’re perfect for the skier who wants to be cozy and stylish after a day on the slopes. —GM.

Industry observers note that lightweight and durable, this everyday helmet is inspired by the speed and precision of ski racing helmets. Equipped with Mips Air Node, BOA Fit System, and advanced adjustable ventilation, the POC Arcus gives you a precise and secure fit with great air flow to keep you cool and comfortable on every run.

Packing for a ski trip can be chaotic, so the more organized, the better. Bonus points if that organization comes in an adorable butter-yellow pouch with ski-themed details. At roughly 9″ W x 6″ H x 4″ D, it’s big enough for all your ski essentials but small enough to fit in any bag. It has already sold out on a few sites, so don’t wait! —Jamie Aranoff, SKI Senior Editor.

Recent findings suggest that ask any kid (or kid at heart) what’s on their holiday wish list, and you’ll likely hear “Jellycat.” These soft creatures come in all shapes and sizes, but the ski-themed critters are downright adorable. From skiing bunnies to spiced mulled cider wearing ski goggles, you’ll be able to find something to make your giftee smile. —JA.

Last season I wore a “Pray for Snow” trucker hat nearly every day, and despite the unironic message, it got tons of compliments. This year, Aviator Nation plastered the iconic phrase on the back of a cozy sweatshirt. The female-founded brand is known for exceptionally soft sweats hand-sewn in Southern California, and there’s nothing better to slip into for après. —JA.

In a recent development, I come from the camp that candles make excellent gifts, especially luxe candles. For anyone who wants their home to smell like fresh snow, this one is a surefire win. With notes of jasmine sambac and warm musk, it’s the kind of candle you secretly want but would never buy for yourself. It also makes a great white elephant gift for skiers and winter lovers. —JA.

Kelly Slater’s co-founded brand Outerknown makes clothing for the life we all wish we lived: calm, cool and California-chic. The brand offers plenty of responsibly sourced cozywear, but the Nostalgia sweater is a hands-down crowd-pleaser. Made from 100 percent organic cotton with a retro rainbow design, it’s the perfect sweater to throw on after a long ski day. —JA.

It seems like out of nowhere, Lola Blankets became the season’s biggest talking point. From billboards to Instagram, these blankets have quite literally taken over. And while there are plenty of dupes out there that look identical, there is something about this blanket that cannot be recreated anywhere else. It is the softest blanket I have ever felt, and that feeling does not diminish with wear. Getting cozy after skiing is a right for all skiers, and if you want to win over any skier’s icy heart, then look no further. —JA.

It has been revealed that last spring, I skied Aspen Highlands’ closing day. After a warm winter, I’d packed light, but it still wasn’t light enough, so I picked up the Hayden Hoodie to wear under a puffer vest. The fleece kept me warm on the snow and blocked some wind without overheating me, and it’s been in heavy rotation all fall. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth wants to build a newly introduced military base, and some public land states like Wyoming say they have just the spots.
  • The base would house between 15,000 and 25,000 active-duty service members, according to a red, white and blue competition flier for what Hegseth is calling the Next Great American Base contest.
  • Recent findings suggest that hegseth remarked the base should be a “dynamic, self-sustaining power projection platform” with its own power generation, modern air defenses, and advanced technology, reported Newsweek in early October, when the call for pitches first arrived.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth wants to build a newly introduced military base, and some public land states like Wyoming say they have just the spots.

The base would house between 15,000 and 25,000 active-duty service members, according to a red, white and blue competition flier for what Hegseth is calling the Next Great American Base contest. And ideally it would include 100,000 to 250,000 contiguous acres.

Recent findings suggest that hegseth remarked the base should be a “dynamic, self-sustaining power projection platform” with its own power generation, modern air defenses, and advanced technology, reported Newsweek in early October, when the call for pitches first arrived. He went on to say the best proposals would cut through “the red tape, offering up the land and rolling out the red carpet for our military families.”.

But much of the “red tape” associated with building a base on hundreds of thousands of acres of unoccupied land is likely federal government red tape. And no clear path at the moment exists for how to requisition and build a new military installation on federal public land, said Mark Squillace, a natural resources law professor at the University of Colorado Law School.

It has been revealed that the Department of Defense would need to work around current Bureau of Land Management or U.S. Forest Service management plans that include stipulations for wildlife like migration corridors and winter range closures.

It has been revealed that it’s also unclear if the base needs to support the U.S. Navy, which would limit public-land options since the bulk of the country’s public lands are in the Interior West like Nevada, Idaho and Utah, though the fact sheet says all locations, even those without water access, are on the table.

The DOD already administers 8.4 million acres in the U.S., but is looking to acquire lands managed by other agencies.

Wyoming, for its part, is eyeing both state and federal land for the base. The state’s adjutant general, Maj. Gen. Greg Porter, told a legislative committee in early November that Wyoming has identified at least four “chunks” of state and federal land, as reported by the Cowboy State Daily last week. Which chunks have not yet been disclosed.

Squillace lined out how building a military base on public land could — or could not — become a reality.

The DOD would first likely need to discuss any public land acquisition with the BLM or Forest Service. If the land use agency agrees that a military base would fit the current land management blueprint, it would need to prepare a draft Environmental Impact Statement that brings up potential complications and confirms compliance with laws like the Endangered Species Act or National Historic Preservation Act.

According to recent reports, “A positive review would likely lead to temporary withdrawal of the land from the operation of certain public land laws (like mining and leasing) that could interfere with the operation of the base,” Squillace claims, while also noting that existing rights would be protected. Any particularly valuable mining claims would have to be bought out in what he describes as a “time consuming and expensive” process.

Read Next: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.

Ultimately, however, Squillace says any large-scale, long-term use of land would likely need to be approved by Congress, “since such transfers of public land are not authorized under law.”  Whether or not the dramatically different Congress to be sworn in next year would green light a public-land transfer requested by Hegseth also remains uncertain.

Not long ago, I drove six hours with the Mancos Shale riding shotgun. That isn’t a buddy’s quirky nickname, as in: Yo, my man Mancos, my Shaley bro, hand me the Doritos and Sour Patch Kids, would ya please? It is in fact a geologic formation, a remarkably friable gray-blue-brown mudstone deposited in the Late Cretaceous, some ninety million years before present, when much of what we today call the American West was inundated by a vast inland sea. To an unsuspecting bystander, a turkey vulture or big-rig trucker, I must have seemed to be a lone soul on a desert road trip, only the radio’s pop divas, evangelical preachers, and static for organization. Wrong. Mile after mile, the Mancos was at my side, catching the corner of my eye, whispering sweet nothings in my ear, keeping me intrigued and entertained.

That’s how it goes across great swaths of Upcoming Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Wyoming, and Utah. The Mancos is here, there, everywhere—an.

#79559. How to Hunt the Best Day of the Rut No. 6: November 21

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1264 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fieldandstream ↗ Open Full Page

How to Hunt the Best Day of the Rut No. 6: November 21

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1264 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that november 21st may be the most-hunted day across North America in 2026, as whitetail hunters in the biggest deer hunting states have open gun seasons, and it’s a Saturday during the rut.
  • Recent findings suggest that the majority of does have been bred across the whitetail’s range at this point, but not all.
  • Related: The 7 Best Days of the 2026 Whitetail Rut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that november 21st may be the most-hunted day across North America in 2026, as whitetail hunters in the biggest deer hunting states have open gun seasons, and it’s a Saturday during the rut. One thing is for sure: Millions of hunters will be hitting the woods on this day for a chance to surprise an unsuspecting buck. Meanwhile, this should give well-positioned hunters a chance to intercept deer bouncing from open timber to hidden thickets and everywhere in between. So, dial in that rifle or slug gun for our first firearm-focused Best day of the Whitetail Rut. Below are two high-odds intends that will help get you ready for some action faster than your grandad’s Winchester repeater.

Recent findings suggest that the majority of does have been bred across the whitetail’s range at this point, but not all. Bucks are now searching for those last stragglers, increasing their range to fringe and even newly introduced areas to find them. These “zombie bucks,” running on fumes after weeks of searching all-out for mates, can be seen wandering the landscape at any time of day now. Also, areas with buck-to-doe ratios skewed towards does give hunters an extended chance, as this dynamic prolongs the rut due to the sheer volume of does in the breeding pool. And yes, the influx of hunters in the woods should provide an extra incentive for bucks to be on the move, too, as they flee the increased human presence for their most secluded haunts. For savvy hunters, these are notable clues about where and how to hunt for your best chance of intercepting one of those grizzled old bucks who have dodged arrows and bullets thus far.

Related: The 7 Best Days of the 2026 Whitetail Rut.

Recent findings suggest that one way to gauge hunting pressure at this point in the season is to consider what well-known land specialist Tony LaPratt calls the “doe clock,” in your area. If does are arriving at food sources later and later in the evening, this indicates high pressure and reveals how close to security cover you need to hunt to catch late-rut activity. If does are on a normal schedule, hunt deer patterns as usual. If not, it’s now time to think like a doe who has been running into human traffic in all the usual places and beat her to where she feels most protected—those nasty, impenetrable thickets.

In a recent development, thick tangles, swampy humps, isolated brushy sanctuaries are your go-to spots now. On public land, the best proposal is to get in early and let the droves of hunters push deer to these safe zones and right to you. This is when it’s crucial to beat the other hunters out and be willing to go where they won’t. Take a boat, strap on waders, or crawl, if you must, to access these hidden whitetail havens. A precise-shooting gun that you are confident can thread the needle at moment’s notice shines in these circumstances, where bucks weave in and out of small openings searching for and chasing does, requiring quick target acquisition and exact shots.

According to recent reports, if a thicket isn’t accessible, or if you don’t want to invade your set-aside sanctuary on private land, finding escape routes from neighboring properties leading to isolated cover will pay substantial dividends. This is a tactic my father and uncles used exclusively in the 60s and 70s with great success in Northern Michigan, and it’s just as valid today during a majority of gun seasons around the country. Map where pressure will be, do some homework to find likely entry routes of other hunters, and set up along the quickest and most secure routes deer can take to bedding thickets.

If you’re in a mixed ag region, standing corn becomes a magnet for deer activity in late November. At this time of year, most corn has been harvested, leaving minimal cover and amplifying the drawing power of these last patches of security. A well brushed-in popup blind and a short-barreled slug gun or straight-wall rifle are smart choices. Standing corn allows for screened access along the side of the rows, but be ready. Quick flurries of hooves, hide, and antlers are common.

According to recent reports, and on windy days, stalking your way through a corn field is a great way to sneak up on a bedded buck that just won’t budge. Keep the wind in your face or crossing to your weak side, step across rows looking toward your strong side-shot. Complete a zig-zag pattern every 25 yards or so as you cross rows and weave through the field.

Sources indicate that yes, the rut is about bucks chasing does, but food comes into play more and more as it lingers on. Temperatures begin to dip in many regions, causing both does and bucks to increasingly seek high-energy foods. And again, where the does will be, the bucks will also be, still with breeding at top of mind. Combining both is a dynamite choice for an evening sit.

In a recent development, as a general rule, think greens for warmer days (clover, chicory, tops of turnips, and radishes),  and when it’s cold, think grains (cut corn, beans, wheat, oats, brassica bulbs, or even red oak acorns). But even better, let the deer tell you what they presently prefer. Hopefully you’ve kept some of your food sources off-limits for hunting until now. Use a long-range elevated position like a box blind for easy entry and exit while hunting these destination foods. Prep these locations for all day sits, making sure doors and windows are quiet and able to seal to keep both sound and scent to a minimum.

Another long-range option for this time of year is sitting a major funnel. Especially for areas of the country with low deer populations and large expanses of open land, hard pinch points become an inevitable location that massive bucks will eventually pass through as they scour the landscape for remaining estrus does. According to author and rut-funnel guru Bobby Worthington, persistence is key once these funnels are identified. A few funnels that can work exceptionally well include: a creek crossing where steep banks keep deer from crossing at other locations, strategic hinge-cuts on private land, gates or opening in fenced field areas, necks around bodies of water, and narrow creek bottoms connecting larger timbered areas. Just be aware of “bridges to nowhere,” according to Worthington. These are apparent funnels, but upon looking at the larger landscape don’t really connect anything of significance for deer.

Sources indicate that if deer are dug in like ticks and refuse to move, consider trying a good old-fashioned push, or deer drive, to roust them. Yes, drives are controversial in some circles due to their intrusive nature, so I suggest waiting until after gun season openers and during midday to respect other hunters, especially on public land. Most are familiar with the standard drive where posters stand and drivers crash through large chunks of land sending deer bolting in every direction. I prefer a subtler approach that produces less stress on the deer herd and better shot opportunities—namely, two-man drives. The stander can get a vantage point, even utilizing mobile gear to get up a tree in known pinches, while the pusher slowly works through bedding areas, using the wind to do work for him. These make for slower escapes of deer, fewer running shots, and more opportunities that flying lead will connect with a buck instead of a tree.

  • Sources indicate that “I put in for the early two-day hunt on November 16 and 17 at a Northeast Indiana state park and got drawn for it,” Mike Miltroka tells Outdoor Life.
  • Miltroka found a likely spot and, well before daybreak on Monday, he was in a tree saddle with his Ruger American Generation II chambered in 7mm PRC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that indiana’s state park system offers a limited draw hunt that allows residents to target the abundant whitetails on park land that doesn’t get much hunting pressure. There are about 25 parks in the popular program, with two firearms hunts allowed on most of them. Each hunt runs just two days.

Sources indicate that “I put in for the early two-day hunt on November 16 and 17 at a Northeast Indiana state park and got drawn for it,” Mike Miltroka tells Outdoor Life. “Trail cameras are not allowed on park [land]. But you can scout before hunt days. I scouted the park on Sunday, the day before the first day of hunting on November 16.”.

Miltroka found a likely spot and, well before daybreak on Monday, he was in a tree saddle with his Ruger American Generation II chambered in 7mm PRC.

According to recent reports, “It was cool and a little windy, but I was seeing deer soon after daybreak,” notes Miltroka, a 38-year-old long-haul truck driver from Farmland. “I spotted a good buck far out, but the cover was too thick to shoot.”.

Sources indicate that as the morning wore on, Miltroka got a chance to take two does, and he dropped them both with his Ruger. He toted both does to his truck using a deer cart, since motorized vehicles are not allowed off-road.

The spot was already paying off, and Miltroka had a friend — who had seen a giant deer using the area before the hunt — to thank for tipping him off about it.

“I’d never seen the deer previously, but a buddy indicated me a video [he’d taken] of the buck a month earlier while visiting the park … It was a place no one else was hunting, and I checked to make sure it was okay to hunt there – and it was.”.

According to recent reports, on the second day of the hunt, Miltroka chose a different tree. He climbed into a big walnut closer to the cover where he’d seen the buck on Monday. But unlike the day before, Miltroka didn’t see much except a coyote. Then, around 8:30, things changed.

“I heard something raking trees behind me, and I didn’t know what it was. I kept trying to see what was making all that racket, then I saw him out about 70 yards,” he indicates. “I knew it was a good shooter buck, and when I got him in my scope I squeezed the trigger, fired, and the deer took off running.”.

Miltroka jacked another round into the chamber, but as soon as he picked up the running buck in his scope again, the deer went down.

It wasn’t until Miltroka studied the dead buck through his scope that he realized how immense the deer was.

“I started shaking, and yelling,” he says. “I got buck fever after it was over … I called a friend of mine and was so excited he asked if I was tied tight to my tree, and I remarked yes. I was shaking so much I might have fallen out of it.”.

Once he was steady enough, Miltroka climbed down and walked up on the deer.

“I was in complete shock,” he indicates. “I’ve only taken about six bucks, and none even have the size of this one. I was screaming with joy.”.

He filled out a transport tag for his buck, which filled his limit of three deer for the park hunt – only one of which can be a buck. Then he wheeled the buck to his vehicle, loaded it, and drove to park headquarters to check it in.

It has been revealed that the buck’s field dressed weight was 181 pounds. The 22-point nontypical was green scored by an official Boone & Crockett measurer the day after Miltroka shot it. It gross scored 227 inches, with a net score of 197 6/8s inches. It has an outside antler spread of nearly 25 inches, and one main beam of the rack measures over 27 inches.

It has been revealed that he will have the buck scored again after the required 60-day drying period for B&C and will enter the buck into B&C’s nontypical record category. He’ll also submit his buck to the Hoosier Record Buck Program.

It has been revealed that “The park hunts are well run and there are plenty of deer,” says Miltroka. “I saw lots of deer being checked in during the hunts and some nice bucks.

“I’m stunned at the size of my deer. But there are so many great bucks that have come from Indiana.”.

Baboons are assholes. After leaving his birth troop at around age seven, a male will find a newly introduced one and spend his prime years trying to fang his way up the hierarchy. Once he’s gained a modicum of status, he devotes his days to terrorizing lower-ranking males and females, who only grow to half his size. Gashes, puncture wounds, and missing ears are not uncommon among baboons.

In the mid-1980s, Dr. Robert M. Sapolsky, a primatologist living in Kenya, documented an unprecedented cultural shift when he noticed that the alpha males of a baboon population suddenly vanished. The alphas had come upon a garbage dump near a tourist lodge, and they defended their spoils furiously from low-ranking males and females, who were relegated to leaves, seeds, and insects on the forest floor. #79555. I Went Duck Hunting During the Infamous Armistice Day Storm, and Lived to Tell About It

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3087 w)
